title: Series & Parallel
description: Combine resistors in series and in parallel to simplify a network step by step.

study.title: Resistors in series
study.body: Elements are in **series** when the same current must flow through all of them: they are connected end to end, with nothing else attached at the joints. Series resistances simply add, so the equivalent is always **larger** than the largest resistor.

study.title: Resistors in parallel
study.body: Elements are in **parallel** when both of their ends connect to the **same two nodes**, so they share the same voltage. Their conductances add, so the reciprocals of the resistances add. The equivalent is always **smaller** than the smallest resistor.

study.title: Two in parallel: product over sum
study.body: For exactly two resistors there is a shortcut. Special cases: $n$ equal resistors $R$ in parallel give $R/n$, and a resistor in parallel with a much larger one is almost unchanged (1 kΩ ∥ 1 MΩ ≈ 999 Ω). Product over sum works for **two** resistors only — for three, combine two first, then add the third.

study.title: Reducing a network
study.body:
To find the resistance between two terminals, start **farthest from the terminals** and work towards them:
- find a group that is clearly in series or in parallel
- replace it by its equivalent and redraw
- repeat until one resistor remains
At every step check: series = same current, parallel = same two nodes.

study.title: Worked example
study.body:
Between a and b: $R_1$ = 1 kΩ in series with ($R_2$ = 6 kΩ ∥ $R_3$ = 3 kΩ).
- $R_2 \parallel R_3$ = (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2 kΩ
- $R_{eq}$ = 1 kΩ + 2 kΩ = 3 kΩ
With 12 V applied, the source current is 12 V / 3 kΩ = 4 mA, the parallel pair has 4 mA × 2 kΩ = 8 V across it, and $R_3$ carries 8 V / 3 kΩ = 2.67 mA.

study.title: Pitfalls
study.body:
- Two resistors that share only **one** node are not automatically in series: a third element at that node takes away current.
- A resistor with an ideal wire (short circuit) across it carries no current; replace the pair by the wire.
- A resistor with one end left open (dangling) carries no current and does not affect $R_{eq}$.
- A source connected to a network sees $R_{eq}$, so its current is $V_s/R_{eq}$.

steps.title: Series: one path
steps.body: Resistors are in **series** when they are connected end to end, so the **same current** flows through each. Their resistances simply add — a longer obstacle course for the charge.

steps.prompt: What is the equivalent resistance between a and b?
steps.explanation: Series resistances add: $R_{eq}$ = {{R1}} + {{R2}} + {{R3}} = {{R1+R2+R3|Ω}}.

steps.title: Parallel: side by side
steps.body: Resistors are in **parallel** when both ends connect to the **same two nodes**, so they share the **same voltage**. Extra paths make it easier for current to flow, so the equivalent resistance **drops**. For two resistors use product over sum.

steps.prompt: What is the equivalent resistance between a and b?
The equivalent resistance of two resistors in parallel is always…
steps.explanation: Adding a parallel path can only make it easier for current to flow. Even the smallest resistor alone would carry some current; with the other in parallel, more current flows for the same voltage, so $R_{eq}$ is below the smallest value.

steps.title: Spotting series and parallel
steps.body:
- **Series**: end to end with **nothing else** attached at the joint, so the same current flows through both.
- **Parallel**: both ends on the **same two nodes**, so they have the same voltage.
Two resistors can also be neither! Here $R_2$ and $R_3$ share both nodes, and that pair is in series with $R_1$.

steps.prompt: Look at this network again. Which statement is true?
options: $R_2$ and $R_3$ are in parallel, and that pair is in series with $R_1$
All three resistors are in parallel
steps.explanation: $R_2$ and $R_3$ both connect the top-right node to the bottom wire: parallel. $R_1$ and $R_2$ are **not** in series, because $R_3$ is also attached at their joint and takes part of the current. The current through $R_1$ is the total current into the pair, so $R_1$ is in series with $R_2 \parallel R_3$ as a whole.

steps.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance between a and b.
steps.explanation:
First the parallel pair: $R_2 \parallel R_3$ = ({{R2}} × {{R3}}) / ({{R2}} + {{R3}}) = {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}}.
Then add $R_1$ in series: $R_{eq}$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} = {{R1+par(R2,R3)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: {{n}} identical {{R|Ω}} resistors are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance?
steps.explanation: Each resistor has conductance $1/R$; {{n}} of them give $n/R$. So $R_{eq} = R/n$ = {{R|Ω}} / {{n}} = {{R/n|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance between a and b.
steps.explanation:
$R_1$ and $R_2$ carry the same current (nothing else is attached between them): series, {{R1|Ω}} + {{R2|Ω}} = {{R1+R2|Ω}}.
That branch and $R_3$ connect the same two nodes: parallel.
$R_{eq}$ = ({{R1+R2}} × {{R3}}) / ({{R1+R2}} + {{R3}}) = {{par(R1+R2,R3)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance of the three parallel resistors.
What is {{R1|Ω}} in parallel with {{R2|Ω}}?
steps.explanation: Product over sum: ({{R1}} × {{R2}}) / ({{R1}} + {{R2}}) = {{par(R1,R2)|Ω}}. Adding them ({{R1+R2|Ω}}) would be series, and the average is not a circuit rule at all. Check: the result must be smaller than {{min(R1,R2)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Which resistor $R_2$ must be placed in parallel with $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} to obtain {{Req|Ω}}?
What current does the source deliver?
steps.explanation:
The source sees $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3)|Ω}} = {{R1+par(R2,R3)|Ω}}.
$i_s = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{Vs}} V / {{R1+par(R2,R3)|Ω}} = {{Vs/(R1+par(R2,R3))|A}}.

steps.prompt: Three resistors with conductances {{G1|S}}, {{G2|S}} and {{G3|S}} are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent **resistance**?
steps.explanation:
Conductances in parallel add: $G_{eq}$ = {{G1|S}} + {{G2|S}} + {{G3|S}} = {{G1+G2+G3|S}}.
$R_{eq} = 1/G_{eq}$ = {{1/(G1+G2+G3)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Two resistors that share one node are always in series.
steps.explanation: They are in series only if **nothing else** is connected at that shared node, so that the same current must flow through both. If a third element is attached there, it takes part of the current and the two resistors are not in series.

steps.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance between a and b. Start at the far end!
steps.explanation:
1. $R_3$ and $R_4$ are in series: {{R3+R4|Ω}}.
2. That branch is in parallel with $R_2$: ({{R2}} × {{R3+R4}}) / ({{R2}} + {{R3+R4}}) = {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}.
3. Add $R_1$: $R_{eq}$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}} = {{R1+par(R2,R3+R4)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: A resistor is added **in parallel** with an existing network. The equivalent resistance of the network…
steps.explanation: The new resistor adds an extra path, i.e. extra conductance: $G_{eq}$ grows, so $R_{eq} = 1/G_{eq}$ drops. (Adding a resistor in **series** would increase it.)

steps.prompt: Tap every resistor that is in **parallel** with $R_3$.
steps.explanation: $R_2$ and $R_3$ connect the same two nodes (top junction and bottom rail), so they are in parallel. $R_4$ is in series with $R_5$, and that pair is in parallel with $R_3$ as a whole, but $R_4$ and $R_5$ individually are not. $R_1$ carries the full source current, so it is in series with the rest.

steps.prompt: Tap every resistor that is in **series** with $R_1$ (it carries exactly the same current).
steps.explanation:
Follow the current that enters at a. It passes $R_1$ and then $R_2$ with nothing else connected at their joint, so $R_1$ and $R_2$ carry the same current. At the junction it splits between $R_3$ and the branch $R_4$–$R_5$, and it recombines before flowing through $R_6$ back to b. So **all** of the current also passes through $R_6$: $R_6$ is in series with $R_1$, even though it is drawn on the other side.
$R_4$ and $R_5$ are in series with each other, and that pair is in parallel with $R_3$.

steps.prompt: Terminal c is left open. Tap every resistor you could cut out of the circuit **without changing** $R_{ab}$.
steps.explanation:
- $R_3$ is shorted by the wire drawn above it: its two ends are the same node, so it carries no current and removing it changes nothing.
- $R_5$ leads only to the open terminal c. No current can flow through it, so it does not take part either.
What remains is $R_{ab} = R_1 + (R_2 \parallel R_4)$. Removing $R_1$, $R_2$ or $R_4$ would change that.

steps.prompt: Find the equivalent resistance between a and b of this ladder network.
All values are shown in the schematic.
steps.explanation: Reduce the network: $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{R1+Rp|Ω}}, so the source current is $i_s = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{is|A}}. Then work back: $v_1 = i_sR_1$ and the parallel pair has $v_p = i_s(R_2 \parallel R_3)$ = {{is*Rp|V}}.

ask.explanation:
1. $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{Rp|Ω}} = {{R1+Rp|Ω}}.
2. Source current: $i_s = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{is|A}}.
3. Voltage across the parallel pair: $v_p = i_s(R_2 \parallel R_3)$ = {{is*Rp|V}}.
4. $i_3 = v_p/R_3$ = {{is*Rp|V}} / {{R3|Ω}} = {{abs(I_R3)|A}}.

1. $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{Rp|Ω}} = {{R1+Rp|Ω}}.
2. Source current: $i_s = V_s/R_{eq}$ = {{is|A}}; all of it flows through $R_1$.
3. $v_1 = i_sR_1$ = {{is|A}} × {{R1|Ω}} = {{abs(V_R1)|V}}.

ask.prompt: Find the power delivered by the source.
ask.explanation:
The source sees $R_{eq} = R_1 + R_2 \parallel R_3$ = {{R1+Rp|Ω}}.
$P = V_s^2/R_{eq}$ = {{Vs}}² / {{R1+Rp}} = {{P_Vs|W}} (or $V_s i_s$ with $i_s$ = {{is|A}}).

steps.prompt: How much power does the source deliver to this ladder network?
steps.explanation:
Reduce from the right: $R_4 \parallel R_5$ = {{par(R4,R5)|Ω}}; + $R_3$ = {{R3+par(R4,R5)|Ω}}; ∥ $R_2$ = {{par(R2,R3+par(R4,R5))|Ω}}; + $R_1$ = {{Req|Ω}}.
$P = V_s^2/R_{eq}$ = ({{Vs}} V)² / {{Req|Ω}} = {{Vs^2/Req|W}}.

steps.prompt: A network consists of $R_1$ = {{R1|Ω}} in series with ($R_2$ = {{R2|Ω}} ∥ $R_x$). Which $R_x$ gives a total of {{Rt|Ω}}?
steps.explanation:
1. The parallel part must be $R_p = R_{total} - R_1$ = {{Rt|Ω}} − {{R1|Ω}} = {{Rt-R1|Ω}}.
2. From $\frac{1}{R_p} = \frac{1}{R_2} + \frac{1}{R_x}$: $R_x = \frac{R_2R_p}{R_2 - R_p}$ = ({{R2}} × {{Rt-R1}}) / ({{R2}} − {{Rt-R1}}) = {{R2*k/(1-k)|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: The vertical line in the middle is an ideal wire. What is the resistance between a and b?
steps.explanation: The wire connects the top node directly to the bottom wire, so $R_2$, the wire and $R_3$ are all in parallel. Anything in parallel with 0 Ω gives 0 Ω: $R_2$ and $R_3$ carry no current. Only $R_1$ remains: $R_{ab}$ = {{R1|Ω}}.

steps.prompt: Terminal c is left open (nothing is connected to it). What is the resistance between a and b?
steps.explanation: With terminal c open, no current can flow through $R_3$ — it is a dead end, and it does not change $R_{ab}$. The current from a flows through $R_1$ and then $R_2$ to b: $R_{ab}$ = {{R1|Ω}} + {{R2|Ω}} = {{R1+R2|Ω}}.
